synopsis: The booklet treats a fallback as a pre-planned, less ambitious but responsible outcome that preserves safety when the main plan cannot be delivered on time; it should be designed before optimism pressure peaks and costed and funded alongside the main plan [f12465, f9691, f12469]. Every decision gate should permit at least four outcomes—go, go with restrictions, pivot or fallback, and stop—with an illustrative independent readiness gate in April 2027 [f9687, f9655]. The preferred release fallback restricts automatic braking to an operating envelope where the safety case is closed, potentially split by machine family, while retaining warning-only behavior outside that envelope; incomplete safety evidence warrants delaying brake control rather than exposing operators to unresolved uncertainty [f14865, f12326, f10998]. The descoping ladder reduces scenario classes, then narrows the operating envelope, then substitutes decision-support evidence for safety-case evidence; off-ramps include physical tests for highest-integrity claims, simulation limited to screening, and engineering-learning rather than safety-credit results [f9693, f12468]. Planning should identify scope-reduction dates and report P50/P80 dates and deadline probability for August or September 2027 deliverables, but the four-month target remains a business objective rather than a pass criterion: full scope should be delayed rather than supported by indefensible virtual equivalence [f10250, f10151, f12478].
